docs.inserted:
2. | When the package is a project in a local directory, expect the
        checkout to be left exactly as it was after
        ``pip install ./myproject`` -- there are no ``build/`` or
        ``.egg-info`` directories to add to ``.gitignore`` or clean up
        between builds.
docs.why_implied: The sentence only tells the reader what to expect after installing a local project (a pristine checkout, nothing to gitignore). That is only true when pip copied the project to a temporary directory before building; since pip now invokes the build system in place, backends such as setuptools leave build/ and .egg-info in the project directory. The reader must connect 'nothing appears in the checkout' to the build location.

docs.inserted:
``search`` sits directly under ``Command`` because it never builds a
``PackageFinder`` or reads Simple API pages: it sends a single query to the
index's search API and prints the names and summaries that come back, so a
bare ``pip search <term>`` with no ``--index`` option simply lists the
matching projects.
docs.why_implied: The insertion describes what a user will see from a bare `pip search` (a list of matching projects). With no --index, the command targets PyPI, and PyPI no longer supports XML-RPC search, so today the command fails there. The reader has to know the default index is PyPI and that PyPI dropped search; the sentence never says PyPI supports it.

docs.inserted:
If you do build a locking tool on top of `--report`, validate the `install` array
before writing a lock: for each item, evaluate its `requires_dist` entries against the
`environment` markers, check that the version recorded for every dependency they name
satisfies them, and refuse to lock when one does not, since the report keeps the first
version pip settled on for a shared dependency even when a requirement it reached later
asked for a different one.
docs.why_implied: The step (re-validate the install set for mutually unsatisfied requirements before locking) and its rationale (first version settled on is kept even if a later requirement disagrees) only make sense under the legacy resolver's first-found-wins behaviour. With the default backtracking resolver the resolved set is consistent or pip errors with ResolutionImpossible. No resolver name, 'legacy' or 'backtracking' appears; the reader must infer which resolver the step presupposes.

docs.inserted:
For example, with ``python3.9 -m pip download --only-binary=:all: numpy``
the ``cp39`` wheels are the relevant links, and wheels built for other CPython
versions are skipped.
docs.why_implied: The example command runs current pip under CPython 3.9. Current pip supports only CPython 3.10-3.15 (plus latest PyPy3), so this invocation no longer works with the pip these docs describe. No prose claims 3.9 is supported; the reader must notice the interpreter version in the command line and compare it with the supported range.

docs.inserted: If you are still passing `--use-deprecated=legacy-resolver` in your own workflows, bear in mind that the legacy resolver is deprecated and unsupported, so the `--force-reinstall` behaviour you see with it may not match what is described or recommended here.
docs.why_implied: Conditional on still using the legacy resolver; it restates that the legacy resolver is deprecated and unsupported, which is true today, and asserts nothing false about the current default.

docs.inserted: Had pip still been running its pre-2020 resolver by default, the recursive, one-dependency-after-another picture in several of the answers below would have been a fair description of what pip does; with the backtracking resolver, pip may go back and swap out a version it has already picked when a later requirement conflicts with it.
docs.why_implied: A counterfactual ('Had pip still been running its pre-2020 resolver by default...') that is consistent with the backtracking resolver being the default today; the description of backtracking is accurate.

docs.inserted:
Because PyPI no longer answers ``pip search`` queries, checking for newer
   releases from the terminal means using ``--outdated`` (or :ref:`pip index`),
   which reads the same index pages as ``pip install`` does.
docs.why_implied: True today: PyPI dropped XML-RPC search, so `pip search` cannot be used to look up the latest version on PyPI; `pip list --outdated` and `pip index` use the Simple API / PackageFinder, which PyPI still serves.
Unmodified excerpt about pip's Configuration class; says nothing about supported Python versions, pip search, resolver or local builds.
